My hon. friend goes further, and says that we are not doing all that should be done, but he does not suggest anything more that we could do, or ought to do, but moves his resolution in such a wav that he knows that it must be taken as a vote of want of confidence.
Not necessarily.

Yes, my hon. friend's opening remarks suggest that. He points out that there is going to be a big delegation of farmers here this week, and I do not think I am uncharitable in suggesting that he has brought up this discussion at this time so that he may bring his proposition specially to* the attention of that delegation.
Not at all.

I say that the government is prepared to believe that the country would be greatly benefited by the establishment of abattoirs and by an efficient system of cold storage under government supervision. But I also say that the preservation of the products is being looked after, that the transportation of these products is being properly carried on, that these products are being landed in the

British market in the best possible condition, and that the government is giving immediate and effective consideration and attention to this- very important subject. I am sorry, therefore, that I cannot accept the resolution of the hon. gentleman, but shall have to vote against it, and ask the House to go into Committee of Supply.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the speech of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. In the main he agrees with the proposition of the hon. gentleman who has moved the motion. If I were to be reminiscent, I would refer to the fact that some four years ago the hon. minister took exactlv the same attitude towards a speech on the address made by the hon. member for Huron East (Mr. Chisholm) in the session of 1906, on the question of cold storage which showed a great deal of attention to the subject and gave many valuable suggestions. The minister on that occasion said he agreed largely with the object of the hon. member's speech. He also agrees with the hon. member who has moved the present resolution. He is what we might call a stand-patter; he Is just standing where he was four years ago. I have heard a story about a stand-patter which I think I ought to tell the House. At the time of the flood, after it had rained twenty days and twenty nights, Noah saw a man outside. He opened the door and said: 'Will you come in?' The man said: 'Oh, no, I do not. think there is going to be much of a shower.' That man was the grandfather of the stand-patters; he must have been some relation of the Minister of Agriculture. Now, this country wants something better than stand-patters. The idea of talking of this country consuming the products of this country. No country would be doing its duty in an agricultural sense if it consumed its own products. As an agricultural country we must be a large exporter of the products of the farm. It is all very well to say the population of this country is 8,000,000 and they will eat so much and therefore we will produce so much. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman has so enlarged the stomachs of the people of this country that they are eating two pounds of butter where they used to eat one.
If you take the trouble to go into this question, and look up the facts, you will find that at a certain time in this country and the United States, the people ate more pork, bacon and mutton than they do today. But the hon. minister tells us that they are now much better off, because they are eating more sugar, and all those other articles, which of necessity, cost them less. Milk, he said, is a very expensive diet, hut if he knew anything about poor people as I do, he would know that if you use milk, 394	'
you can feed more people cheaper than in any other way. Of course I quite understand that the hon. gentleman can afford an expensive housekeeper, but I want a woman who will get a good meal at the least expense, and every good housekeeper knows that you can make a family more comfortable with less expense if you use milk freely, so that there is not much in the argument that milk is an expensive luxury.
In order to ascertain how much butter, cheese and milk is produced, the hon. gentleman takes our population at seven millions and a half and estimates that each member of a family consumes per year $10 worth of these products, which would make $75,000,000, and adding to that the-$25,000,000 which we export, you have $100,000,000. But he could make our production still larger, if he would .say that each family consumed at the rate of $15 per annum, per person. There is no real basis; to his calculation; it is founded on the imaginary supposition that the people will eat so much. But when he says that a family of five or eight people will eat $10 per head of these products, he is altogether astray, because they will not get that much. In fact the minister is at his wits end to find some excuse for the falling off in the export of these articles. But all through the country, wherever you find people gathered together, discussing these matters, invariably you will find a friend of the hon. gentleman giving as the reason for the falling off of our exports that we are consuming more at home. In the province of Quebec we have these hon. gentlemen saying that there are 800,000 milch cows, but that is purely imaginary, and is not based on anything real. They say that the average product would be $30 per head, which would give $24,000,000 worth. But how many cattle have you in Canada, and how many milch cows? It is rather strange that in this country we have the number of cattle pretty nearly up to the number of our population. In the United States, with their eighty-five to ninety million people, they hgve only 71,000,000 cattle. What does that mean? It means, if we draw a comparison, that there is a falling off in the products of the country which are most required in the interests of the people generally. Let me give the hon. gentleman some figures which are reliable. The Ontario provincial government has for years, had a system of collecting statistics, which can be depended on. And according to these statistics, we have less cattle in Ontario, by 100,000, than we had three years ago, and we have 65,000 less milch cows than three years ago. I venture to say, that the same thing would be found in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. If you say that we are producing less because we have now fewer milch cows than we

had three years ago, you will be accounting for a good deal of the deficits in our exports, and that will be more reliable than to say it is due to the increased consumption among our people. In bulletin No. 106, issued by the Ontario Department of Agriculture, I find these figures.
How does the Ontario government obtain these figures?

Through, the municipal machinery in that province, from 'their assessors and from inquiries they send out. This has been going on several years. Here is another very strange thing to which I will call attention. There are 51 counties in Ontario, and out -of those there are only 14 that have more milch cows than other cattle. In other words, there are 37 counties in Ontario, which have less milch cows than other cattle, which shows a falling off. Dundas oounty is one, and I may say that Dundas is the largest producer per acre of any county in the Dominion- $4.26 per acre in cheese and butter, nearly double any other county in the Dominion. The next county is Erontena'c, which has more milch cows than other cattle. Glengarry, Grenville, Hastings, Lanark, Lennox and Addington,i Oxford, Prescott, Prince Edward, Russell, Stormont and the county of York. What surprises me, is that when I go to the very home of this industry in western Ontario, I find it shows a falling off. You come down to the Belleville district, which was the centre of this industry, and you find there, also a falling off and the eastern district of Brockville is now where the largest part of that industry is settled. There is one thing to be said, and that is, that the reason why this industry is weakening is because the people have difficulty in getting help. You can get help such as the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), is bringing, but they cannot milk the cows, when you do get them. You want people who can milk cows without injuring them. That is a serious problem and one which the Minister of Agriculture ought to deal with. The farmer, however, is largely to blame himself in the matter. The domestic help question can be solved and the Department of Agriculture can assist in the solution of it, if it would urge the people to make homes for the men. Let the hired man raise a family on his employer's farm and the domestic question is solved. Conditions are changed. I can tell the hon. minister and the House that one reason why the people are gathering into the cities and towns is that the farmer gives a man his home for six months during the hurried time of summer and harvest and turns him adrift in the fall, and he has to go to the city or town to find maintenance and a place to live. The work in the woods is gone Mr. BRODER.
in the older parts of the country, work that gave the people employment and income in winter. Conditions having so greatly changed, the whole system must be changed if we are to keep this bodyf politic in a healthy condition.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I was giving reasons why -we had reduced exportation of some of our important products. I was showing by data that I consider well authenticated that in the province of Ontario, for instance, we were exporting a good many less cattle than in previous years. Two years ago, most of us will remember, we had a severe drought through a large portion of Ontario, and that led to a considerable reduction in the number of cattle wintered over. I do not say that that was an unmixed evil, because it resulted in weeding out from the herds many that might not be considered paying animals. I venture to say that, judging even from the minister's own report, that same condition prevailed to a considerable extent in other parts of the country as wrell. that we are justified in coming to a conclusion that they show a situation that the Department of Agriculture ought to deal with. Now there is one thing to be said. I believe it is possible, with the number of milch cows we have in the province of Ontario to confine the remark to that province-to increase the output 50 per cent without increasing the number of cattle; in other words, we have been keeping cattle that have not been paying their way, so to speak. I am glad to say to the credit of the minister that the cow testing business that has been put on foot has been valuable in the inter-; est of that business. It is a thing that will-result in good. Many farmers were not aware that they were keeping non-paying animals in their herds. If I may be allowed, I would like to quote the example of Denmark on this point. In 1864, Denmark was producing only 80 pounds of butter per cow; to-day they are producing 220 pounds per cow,, which shows the possibilities of improvement under intelligent farming. Now, suppose it were possible for this country to increase the product of our cows 50 per cent, we would have a large quantity to export that we have not got to-day. As a country, we must come to the conclusion that if we are going to take our place as feeders of the world, we must become large exporters of all kinds of agricultural produce.
Now, I want to go a little further, and speak of the situation as regards wheat. The minister in his report makes an estimate of the product of wheat in the three western provinces for 1909, which he puts down at 147,482,000 bushels; Ontario, spring and fall together, 16,262,000; Quebec, 1,679,000; the three eastern provinces, 1,320,-
000.	Total, 166,744,000 bushels. I want to say that I think these figures are a little exaggerated. In 1909 we exported 49,267,734 bushels. Now it is the opinion of experts that the people of this country consume for food and seed on an average seven bushels of wheat per capita; that would give us for the 8,000,000 people in this country, 56,000,000 bushels required for home consumption. Taking this quantity and the 49,000,000 exported from the 166,000,000 in round numbers as the total production in 1909, that would leave 61,000,000 bushels of wheat in the hands of the people. I think that is hardly to be expected. It seems to me that the figures are scarcely borne out when we come to apply these rules to them. We have increased our export in some of our products very materially; in others our export has lessened very materially. In 1910 the total export of agricultural products amounted to $94,331,147, in 1906 they were $54,062,327. That is to sav, in the five years we
increased our export of agricultural products by $36,000,000 in round numbers. Now the total increase in wheat exports during the same time was $18,9501)00;-the total increase in the products of wheat, that is, wheat flour, was $8,608,000. Exports of wheat and products of wheat increased $27,500,000. Now the totM exports were $279,000,000, in round numbers, in 1910, and $235,000,000 in 1906, showing an increase in five years of $43,000,000, of which $27,000,000 was for wheat and wheat products alone.
In our exports of provisions, butter, cheese, eggs, ham, bacon, all these important products of this country, have fallen off in five years by $15,000,000. I am sure that not only the minister, but every man in this House must realize that this is a serious matter, for if we lose the place we now hold in the English markets and the markets of the world for these products it will be no easy thing to regain that position in the future. That is one reason why this country should wake up to the position we are in in reference to these products. Another serious feature of the situation is that while the total exports of agricultural products in 1909-10 was $90,000,000, the revenue of this country, the amount taken from the people in customs, excise and other forms of taxation. was $101,000,000, $11,000,000 more than all the exports of -agricultural products. We cannot continue at that rate and fill the position we should as a producing country. We cannot take from the people in revenue more than the exports of the agricultural products of the farm and continue in a healthy financial condition. The United States have paid not only the interest on the enormous debt entailed t>y their war, but have paid their bonds by the excess of their exports of farm products oyer their taxation, and we must come to that position if Canada is to assume -and hold the position that we ought to fill in Canada if Canada is to fill its proper place in the world.
The minister does not seem to encourage very much the proposition of our friend (Mr. Sproule). He says our friend should have suggested something; he has suggested something. He has suggested the necessity of doing something, and now it devolves on the minister and his colleagues to decide what should be done. He suggests that evil exists. The minister admits it, but he says: You have not suggested any remedy. It is not our business to suggest a remedy, but I shall take the liberty of suggesting some remedies. If the installing of cold storage -and abattoirs, as suggested by the resolution, will stimulate the production of these articles, the country runs no risk in doing it. If, by encouraging these things, we can stimulate production, we are justified in making a moderate outlay in attempting t" do it There is no

avocation in this oountry that receives as little financial help as the great agricultural industry. I do not believe the people in this country can be driven or coerced into doing anything, but they will welcome suggestions from the department and will -carry out. as far as possible, what is in the interest of agriculture. We have an object lesson of this in my own district. I was very much pleased in reading the report of the Minister of Agriculture in Quebec to see what they are doing to encourage the raising of good stock and to do those things that go to make agriculture more attractive, more productive and more profitable. I am also glad to see that Ontario, for a good many years, has given a good deal of attention to this question. Lately the present government of Ontario have taken on themselves to send out to the people -experts in the different kinds of farming. I think there are now 14 in the different counties; there are three in Stormont, Dun-das and Glengarry. These men come directly in contact with the people, and that is what must be done if results are to be achieved. Our friend cannot sit here and say: You must worship in Jerusalem or go to hell. You cannot do that.

Order? I supposed that moderate logic was permissible in this House, you must not say:	In this mountain thou shalt worship and no where else. You have got to come down in contact with the people. I do not say that the Dominion Department of Agriculture can come so directly in contact with the people as can be done through the provincial avenues, because the municipal machinery assists in the case of the province. These instructors are attached to the Collegiate Institutes and High Schools as a branch of agriculture, and they go out and instruct the people in tile draining, taking the levels of fields, spraying orchards, killing certain weeds, coming in direct contact daily with the men in" the Mr. BRODER.

My hon. friend might do something that would help the farmers in this Dominion very materially. For instance they h-ave in the United States and also in different countries in Europe what they call soil surveys. In the United States they commenced, I think in 1899, what they call these soil surveys. They have sixty-two experts whom they send out among the people to examine the soil on the farms as to its nature, physical conditions, &c.. and then thev decide within wThat area such and such crops can be most successfully raised. They have surveyed millions of acres in different states, and the people are asking for these surveys in almost every state in the union, particularly in the south. These are things that could be done in this country. Is it not possible for instance to increase the area for apple raising? Why should not eastern Ontario and Quebec increase their apple area? The Macintosh Red and the Fameuse apple can be raised all through the Ottawa valley, while in Quebec there are millions of acres upon which these fruits can be grown. Would it not be wise for the Minister of Agriculture to send out some one to instruct the people and to suggest that this should be done? This would supply a great need. I think my hon. friend will not say that we have not made any suggestions now.
My hon. friend does not know that wre are already doing much of what he suggests.
You are. I never heard of it, your light is under a bushel, because no one has seen it. I know that Mr. McNeill has lectured in reference to fruit-raisin" in Ontario.
He has assistants.
You have not given us what is called the soil survey.
No.
That is an important thing.
Perhaps so, there are many important things.

Now, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are provinces in which fruit can be raised successfully, but unfortunately these two provinces are not keeping pace with their possibilities. Agriculture in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia is not in what you might call a healthy condition, and I find from a report published by an agricultural commission appointed by the New Brunswick government in 1909 that this commission did not find things very satisfactory in that pro-

vince. For instance, they found 3,428 vacant farms; they named the counties in which these farms are vacant, and they even go so far as to say that the statistics published by the federal Department of Agriculture are not reliable. I quote from that report:
' According to the Dominion census of 1901, and this we regret to say is the latest statement that we can accept as at all accurate in regard to the statistics of agriculture here-New Brunswick had 37,583 persons occupying farms and lots, a farm being five acres and over, a lot anything under five acres; the total area occupied was 4,438,937 acres or an average approximately of 118 acres to a person. Of this there were 1,405,616 acres cleared, or about 37 acres per farm, and 894,795 acres in crops, about 24 acres per farm.
Later figures given out by the census department but not taken from actual inquiry do not at all coincide with actual conditions as found by us from inquiry at our various meetings, and so far as crop yields are concerned these figures do not correspond with the returns compiled by the New Brunswick Department of Agriculture, therefore we regret that we are unable to agree with the bulletins recently issued from the census department.
Our information would lead us to believe that the large increases in crop production and in live stock stated by these latest census bulletins are not true.
Instead of an increase in the province of 9,907 horses, of 38,713 cattle, of 69,920 sheep and of 46,848 swine kept upon New Brunswick farms in 1907 as against those kept in 1901, your commissioners found evidence of a decline in cattle and sheep, no evidence of any increase in horses, and swine may be a little more than holding their own.
I do not know how that commission obtained its data, but at all events they seem to be sure that the statistics of the Dominion government are not reliable. Now, the Department of Agriculture should do something to improve these conditions. It is not a pleasant thing to have to deal with figures that show that we are not making progress, but at the same time we must look our difficulties squarely in the face if we are going to deal with them honestly. There has been a little too much eulogy of the Minister of Agriculture, so that he has got into what you might call a fool's paradise. He thinks everything is all right because his friends are eulogizing him all over the country, but it would be well for them to remind him of his faults once in a while. We farmers have very serious problems before us. A great many people say that Canada will repeat the history of the United States; that our great western country will open up, that we will produce enormous quantities of wheat, and that we will become as wealthy and as great as the United States. But let us remember that corn and cotton are the
two greatest wealth producers in the United States, and that cotton will never be grown in Canada while the growing of corn is restricted to a very limited area with us, and so, we must have something else to depend on. We are told that the United States will soon become buyers of our wheat, but let me tell you that the United States are awakening to the condition of things in their country; and if within the next ten years they should, as it is possible for them, double the production of their wheat that will mean 600,000,000 bushels for export. The acreage of the United States is 1,900,947,200 acres and of this there are 838,591,774 acres in the farms and 414,498,477 acres of improved land on the farms. In other words, 50 per cent of the farms of the United States to-day are unimproved. That means that when 50 acres out of every 100 are improved they will double their product, and we need not think that we will sit down here and sell them wheat and other farm products.
The average production of wheat per acre in the United States is to-day from 12i to 13 bushels, and they will have no trouble in increasing it to 25 bushels to the acre. In the last 10 years they have put forth efforts that are telling marvellously in that country. Last year the federal government of the United States spent $14,000,000 in encouraging agriculture, to say nothing of what the individual states have done. The United States are awakening to the position they are in, and they will doubtlessly double their products and become still greater exporters than they are.
I see that the Minister of Agriculture has left the House, and I was going to make some suggestions to him, but he probably has enough now for him to carry out during the course of his natural life. I want to say, Sir, that the federal authority in this country should assist the province in the development of agriculture. They have the best machinery through which to get to the people, and so they can assist the provinces very easily in carrying out this work. The United States federal authorities have assisted the authorities of the different states in the promotion of agriculture, and there are no greater sticklers for state rights than they are. In 1862 an Act of Congress was passed establishing their agricultural bureau, and in 1887 they passed an Act to further carry out the intention of that Act, and in section 2 they say:
Nothing in this Act shall be construed to impair or modify the legal relation existing between any of the state colleges and the governments of the states or territories in which they are resj>ectively located.
The federal government had given larger grants of land and money to the state colleges for the purpose of encouraging agriculture, and hence it is that they

declare that nothin? in their legislation shall interfere with state's rights to control the colleges. Then in section 9 of this Act they say:
These grants are made subject to the legislative assent of said states and territories.
I say, therefore, that it is quite possible for the federal authorities of this Dominion to help the several provinces in carrying out objects which every honest Canadian should have in view, namely, the encouragement of agriculture, and the increasing of our output of agricultural products. I believe, Sir, the country demands this at the hands of those who may control its destinies for the time being.
There is one trouble in this country, and I do not know but the influence of hon. gentlemen opposite has had some-tning to do with it : There are too many men in this country trying to make a living with their coats on. Hon. gentlemen opposite have taught people to live on the state, and a good many of them are doing so. I want to say that the farmers have worked for less wages than any other class, and they have worked early and late to furnish cheap products to feed a hungry world. A prominent man said to me in Montreal: What is happening? I pay more for my butter, eggs, beef, pork and so on '. I said to him : Do you understand that the old farmer has gone out of the hog-pen and has gone into the automobile? He has as good a right to it as you, and he is going to let you pay for your pork and your eggs and your butter, and you should not grumble because the prices of his products have advanced. Why should he not get better prices for his products? He has fed the world cheaply, he has worked for very little wages, and now people grumble because he is getting something for his work. I say Amen to it. Let more fellows get their coats off and go to work, and then we will hear no more of this grumbling The agricultural interests of this country ought to be dealt with in a serious manner. If the minister thinks his department is not able to grapple with the problems before it-and I say advisedly that- it has not done so-and if he or his colleagues cannot suggest anything to improve matters, then get a commission to look into them seriously. The patriotism of hon. gentlemen opposite has gone around the circle of their party's interests rather than the circle of the country's interests ; and until we get big enough to get outside of that party circle and deal patriotically with the interests of this country as an agricultural country, we will not do our duty as Canadian citizens. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that hon. members on this side of the House have no quarrel with the statement of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down to the effect that the Dominion government should do all it can to encourage agriculture. The question is what they should do. At the same time, I think it is more directly the function of the provincial governments to give illustrations of what can be done on the farm than that of the Dominion government, as they are more in touch with local conditions. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that the government of Ontario has done a great deal to illustrate what can be done by better methods of farming. They have been doing that for a great many years, not only directly, but also through the Guelph Agricultural college. The reputation of that institution is worldwide. It is educating young men not only from Ontario and the rest of the Dominion, but from South America, Japan, the United States and other parts of the world. But coming to the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for East Grey, if it means anything, it means that this government shall establish not only cold storage for chilled meat, &c., but also going into the slaughter house business as a government undertaking. Surely, the hon. gentleman does not mean that seriously- that the Minister of Agriculture of the Dominion government shall go into the slaughter-house business in competition with the present slaughter-house or packing people. In the first session that I came to this House a deputation from the west waited on the government to ask it to establish cold storage for the purpose of shipping chilled meat to England and other countries. That is done very largely by Australia and New Zealand, and generally I believe successfully, especially with mutton. But, as the Minister of Agriculture has pointed out, we are in a very different position from those countries to raise sheep. They have very large ranges, and although their sheep sell at what we would consider a very low price, still they make money, because they have large flocks of them and feed them very cheaply. We have a very different system of farming in this country, and we have to accommodate

ourselves to our conditions. I believe that the Minister of Agriculture and his department have done a great deal to assist the shipping not only of animal products but of fruit to the old country in cold storage. This. season they have carried out a number of experiments with fruit, and I believe successfully. What I believe the Minister of Agriculture should do is to distribute the knowledge of these experiments as widely as possible among the farmers and fruit-growers of the Dominion. I quite agree with the minister that it is absolutely impossible to start a chilled meat proposition until there are enough animals slaughtered to have the slaughtering continue daily and constantly. There must be a sufficient supply to keep the men in these institutions constantly employed. You cannot employ them one day and turn them off two or three days ; you cannot employ them one month and let them go another month. There is an expert knowledge required which you cannot get if you only give it intermittent employment, and such knowledge is specially required in these abattoirs as well as in private slaughter houses. If these abattoirs cannot retain those experts, they will lose money. A few years ago there was in Ontario a great commotion among the farmers and a great movement for the establishment of co-operative slaughter houses. I have in my mind three which were started in Ontario, all of which absolutely failed. These three were cooperative or farmers slaughter houses. The farmers thought that a large amount of money was being made by the meat packers and they undertook to go into the business themselves and get the middlemens' profit. Inside of three years, however, nearly all those co-operative concerns absolutely failed in so far as the first capital invested in them was concerned. The first investment of capital disappeared, and any of those establishments which continued to slaughter were those that were taken over by private corporations.
Some one said this afternoon that as soon as the farmers started to grow hogs in quantity, the prices would come down. I have thought a good deal on that subject, as I am interested, as a farmer, in that very question, and I have sometimes wondered if iit were not the case that just as quick as the packers got the farmers to grow a sufficient amount of pork, they combined purposely to put down the prices. Well, I have come to the conclusion that such is not the case. The fact is, that when pork was up to 8, 9 and 9i cts., as it has been during the last two years, the packers were losing money, and the only reason why they continued to buy and slaughter, was because they could not afford to shut down their packing houses. At the present price, no doubt the packers
would get even to a certain extent and the farmers will suffer; but we have to take the bitter with the sweet as every one else has to do in other lines of business. I do not believe that the packers purposely raise the prices in order to encourage the farmers to grow hogs and then cut the prices down; but I believe that just as quick as hogs, cattle or other things go up in price, the farmers rush in and grow them and then the price goes down. It is simply a case of supply and demand. Two years ago I was about the only one in my section growing hogs to any large extent, but this fall everybody was growing them, and in consequence, the price has gone down considerably.
Some one said also this afternoon that Die prices would break in Toronto 25 cents and yet in Chicago and East Buffalo they would go up 5 to 10c. per 100 lbs. Well, I have followed the market as closely as any one in this House, and I do know that last fall, when the prices started going down in Toronto, they did go up once or twice in Chicago and in East Buffalo, but very shortly after they came down again in both these places as well as in Toronto. Why? When the prices were going up 5 to 10 cts., the receipts in Chicago were 10,000 a day, but as soon as the receipts went up to 15,000,	20,000 and
25,000' per day, down went the price in Chicago just as it did in Toronto.
To-day, just as during the past four or five years, so far as Ontario is concerned at any rate, we would be better off if there were no duty on hogs going into 'the United States. There are very few articles growing on the Ontario farms which would not be benefited by a removal of the duty in the United States, because the consumption there has become so large that it absorbs to a very great extent all their animal ^products, although they do export some of these products and do export dead meat.
If the consumption there absorbs all their products, how is it that they exported last year $203,000,000 worth?

I have said that they consume to a very large extent their own animal products, and you will find that the United States export in this line is falling off every year. In fact some of the American statisticians say that by 1915 that export will have entirely disappeared. I am not a prophet nor the son of a prophet and will not vouch for the prediction; but for years I have followed the market, for years I have followed the exports of the United States and Canada, and I do know that the American exports are falling off just as rapidly as ours.
My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). has said that there has

been no falling off in the production of cattle and hogs in this country as compared with 1903, when our exports were at their highest, but that the decrease in the exports was due entirely to the local consumption. From my knowledge of the question, I agree with him. But to make sure I went out to the library and turned up the market quotations in the Toronto daily papers in 1905 and 1910 for the months of September and October. To my surprise I found that in 13 weeks of September and October 1905, there were shipped into Toronto 1,253 car loads of cattle, and in the same period in 1910, 1,845 carloads of cattle. You can judge by these figures whether the Minister of Agriculture was correct in his statement that the Canadian consumption was increasing.
Has the hon. gentleman any knowledge of the_ number of cars that came from the Northwest with cattle to the Toronto market this fall?

I am quite well aware that a great number of these cars came from the Northwest, but I do not see how that affects the argument. We are speaking simply of the Dominion of Canada and that brings me to a most important point, namely, that the farmers of Ontario bought at a very high price all those feeders from Manitoba and the west. They were able to absorb, not only their own stock, but hundreds of carloads of cattle from Manitoba and the west which the farmers of the west could not feed or thought they could not, although I understand that the Manitoba people, after they began to ship, found out that they had more feed than they thought.
As regards the falling off in shipments of butter, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture was exactly right. There is no reason for the falling off except that the farmers, at least of Ontario, have found that it does not pay them to make butter. Labour is too scarce, for one thing. And they are trying to relieve their wives and families of the labour of making butter, for another thing. And the price of cheese has run high, as any hon. member will see who will look back over the market quotations. It pays the farmer of Ontario, and of Canada generally, as well to make cheese as to make butter-yes, and a little better, as I know from experience. Some hon. members' said we did not consume much cheese. But we are consuming more cheese than we used to do. In the last five years, Canada has consumed more cheese than in any ten years before that. Even the farmers themselves are consuming more cheese than they did a few years ago.
The whole question, as I understand the amendment, is whether we should encour-Mr. NESBITT.
age agriculture by having the government go into the packing and chilled meat business. I believe we should assist thd farmers, if we can find a consistent wayf to do it,, in getting their cattle and allj other products to market. And I do not! think any person can find fault with the government on that score, unless he be a very narrow partisan indeed. The government has done a great deal to improve the means of transportation. And, so far as the farmers are concerned, whom I have the honour to represent, all they ask, essentially, is transportation. They don't ask any body to send out soil surveyors for them. The farmers I have the honour to represent know how to survey their own soil. And they know what to grow on their own soil. They would not thank the Minister of Agriculture to send out men to tell them what to grow. They know what their soil will grow and what it will grow most of, and grow most profitably. What they ask this government to do is to see to it that the cars, and not only the cars but the boats, are in well iced and otherwise in condition to take their goods to the English market, or whatever market they are destined for. No man on either side, I believe, can fairly accuse the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) of having failed to put forth his best efforts to fill that want. And I believe he has been successful. Many things crop up in which the minister can assist the farmer. As I have said, I do not doubt that every year, yes, and every day, he sees something in which he can help the farmers to a certain extent. Of course, he is limited by the means placed at his disposal. I have told him frankly that I thought it was money well spent to do anything he can to assist the farmer. The farmers do not want such assistance as a great many hon. gentlemen here ask the government to give. The farmers do not believe in paternal government any more than the manufacturers do. They do not want the Minister of Agriculture to tell them how to run their farms. They do ask that the results of successful experiments made at the Experimental Farms shall be transmitted to them, and transmitted to them individually. They cannot afford, with their limited means, to make experiments themselves, but, when they are told the facts concerning a successful experiment, they are as capable of applying the information as any other class in this country. So far as the farmers of North Oxford are concerned, there are not many of them who are not just as capable of running their farms as any man on the floor of this House, no matter what his education may have been. And they are doing it; they are increasing their output in every way-they are increasing

their beef cattle, their hogs and even their sheep. A good deal has been said this afternoon as to why the farmers of Canada do not grow more sheep. It is a simple matter. In the first place, as the Minister of Agriculture told you, the climate is against it. It means a great deal of care when ewes are lambing, and it is often difficult to raise lambs in this country. But, as soon as lambs reach a price at which it pays the farmers to raise them, you will see how quickly the farmers will increase their flocks of sheep. Last year and the year before were the first years, for some time, at least, when it paid the farmers to raise sheep. This year, many farmers in my section of country got $5 a head in June for their lambs. That paid them well, I never figured it out exactly but I believe that at $5, $5.25 and $5.50 in June and July, the farmers would make a hundred per cent. And, let me tell you, there will be a lot more lambs raised in Oxford next spring than there were last spring and the spring before. Why? Because the prices pay the farmer, and the farmer knows what pays him as well as any hon. member of this House can tell him. As I have said, I believe the Minister of Agriculture was right when he said that there had not been a falling off in the animal products of this country, but, on the contrary, an increase. One reason why I believe that is because there has been an enormous increase in home consumption in the last ten years, not only in meat but in dairy products. And that increase of consumption has not been among the people of the cities only, but among the farmers also. The farmers' are living much better than they did a few years ago, and this fact accounts, in part', for the increased consumption of fowls! eggs, milk, butter, cheese, beef, lamb and' other things that are good to eat. And in our section, at any rate, they are living a^ well as any one.
What about the twelve million pounds of mess pork that come into this country from the United States?

That is heavy pork that goes to the lumber woods, pork that we do not raise here, except some old stags *or sows we do not want any longer. Any man who can raise a hog to 180 or 200 pounds in six months does not need to raise a lot of stags and,sell them off for fat pork-and that is what we get from the other side of the line, to a large extent.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that they are imported from the United States, and then exported?

No, I do not say so. Now, as to this alleged combine of the pork packers to keep down the price of hogs, I
do not believe that there is any such combine. I believe that with hogs at over 8 cents per pound the packers lose money, and that, I think, is very well illustrated, even by the price of bacon. The bacon these packers sell in our own country, I agree, they do not lose money on, because they get a high price in the cities here. But, remember, bacon, is only one part of the hog, not the whole hog by any manner of means. People pay a high price for bacon, and are able to pay it. Go into the clubs, the trains, the hotels, see how many people order bacon for breakfast. It is a credit to the country that there are so many people who can afford it; it was not so a few years ago; there was nothing like the consumption of bacon a few years ago that there is now. But, within the last ten years, or five years at any rate, it has not paid to export bacon with hogs at eight cents per pound or more on foot. Now, as to the Minister of Agriculture and what he ought to do for the farmer, I think, in the first place, this question of chilled meat should be discussed not from a partisan standpoint, but on a commercial basis.
From a farmers' standpoint.

Yes, from a farmers' standpoint, which is a commercial basis. The business cannot stand on any other basis; if it does not pay commercially, it is bound to fail whether run by a government, or run by an individual. A business that cannot be run by individuals and made to pay has a mighty poor chance, in my judgment, to be run by any government and made to pay. I am not speaking from a partisan standpoint. It would not matter if hon. gentlemen opposite were in power to-morrow, they could not take up a business that could not be run by a private corporation on a paying basis and run it successfully as a government. I do not believe the government of this country, or of any country, should go into commercial business. I am that much of an individualist. The ranching industry in Canada is rapidly passing. In Saskatchewan and Alberta the handwriting is already on the wall, and in these provinces it is only a matter of time until even the districts still regarded as unfit for general agriculture will, through modern methods of dry farming or by means of irrigation, be brought under cultivation.
There is no question regarding the truth of the statements of this paragraph of the report of Dr. Rutherford, because this ranch country which at one time extended over perhaps half a million square miles of our province has dwindled down until it is contained in an area of perhaps 10,000 square miles with Medicine Hat in Alberta about the centre of the ranching business. So you may see from the ranching point of view that the handwriting is certainly on the wall and that the industry will very soon be a thing of the past.
This is not a new question, it has been placed before the government on various occasions in the last four or five years, it has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and the government again and again. We are about tired of calling for aid and are almost reconciled to our fate. Our only hope is that a change of government and a new policy may come before the cattle trade in the west-is killed altogether. What we want is a government that will take an interest in the agricultural interests of this country and a Minister of Agriculture who will be ready to see that the farmers of Canada get what they are entitled to. The farming interests constitute a large percentage of our population, it is the producing element of our population and at present the farmers are certainly getting very little recognition from this government, they are not getting what they should get, and I see no hope for the people of our country except a change of government which I think will certainly come on the first opportunity the people have to express their will. It is not only in the west that complaints are being made. Only the other day at a meeting of live-stock men in Guelph it was pointed out that government neglect was killing this great industry in every part of Canada. I take it that the chief aim of a government is not to collect taxation, not to help grafters or friends, but to place the national industries of the country on a sound and stable basis. The stock-raising business is one of the most important industries that a country can possess. Every one knows that unless we soon undertake mixed farming in the west, it will not be many years until we will

The grain-growers are crowding out the ranch-men and cattle-rangers but the grain men will soon need the cattle to restore to the soil the fertility which grain-growing takes away from it. Why is the cattle <and live-stock trade of this country declining? Because the business from an international standpoint is passing through a change in conditions. There has been a great revolution in the trade, in the manner of handling the export of meat and this government has not realized it. New methods must he' adopted if we are to hold our own and succeed. In the old days the cattle were driven off the range, shipped in cars to the seaboard and alive to the old country. Those that were in good condition were killed on arrival and those that were not were sent out to British farms to graze and fatten and were ultimately slaughtered and sold as British beef.
A strong agitation sprang up in the old country against this system. The farmers there wanted protection. Even in free trade England they got their protection under an assumed name. It was claimed that this system endangered the health of British herds, and an embargo was placed on foreign cattle. This was done and all foreign cattle sent to England have to be slaughtered on arrival. This has virtually killed the cattle trade in western cattle.

As soon as the embargo was placed upon cattle other countries began to equip themselves to meet the changed conditions in trade. First to adjust themselves to the changes, came the consuming countries, England, France and Germany. They in-Mr. HERRON.
augurated large systems of cold storage warehouses. The exigencies of the law would not permit of the cattle being held alive in England to meet market conditions, so it was arranged that the beef that was slaughtered would be held for the market, and thus steady prices. It is now estimated that Great Britain passes annually through its cold storage warehouses over a billion dollars worth of meat products. No sooner were these warehouses established in England than foreign shippers of live stock began to realize that it would be much to their own advantage to go into the cold storage business also and kill the cattle at home. Now the bulk of meats shipped from the Argentine Republic and from the United States, that used formerly to be shipped on the hoof, are shipped in cold storage. In both the Argentine Republic and the United States the trade in live stock had been well organized and it was not very hard to get the money to build cold storage and embark in the new business. Private enterprises worked out the problem, but at the same time the business resolved itself into trusts. The ' Big Six ' packing houses now handle all the meat products of the United States, which is said to amount to $1,300,000,000 annually that passes through cold storage for home and foreign shipments. The value of these cold storage warehouses and freezers is placed at $30,000,000. In 1899 the trade had required 9,164 cars. Now there are over 100,000 refrigerator cars in use.
In the Argentine Republic the ' Big Eight ' companies do the chilled meat trade, both domestic and foreign. This foreign chilled meat trade in 1907 amounted to" $40,000,000, an increase in seven years of $32,000,000. The live stock export trade in 1900 amounted only to $8,444,410. It will thus be seen that cold storage in the Argentine in less than ten years has increased exports 500 per cent.
In the days when cattle were shipped into Great Britain on the hoof - from Canada, the Argentine and United States, the Australian and New Zealand trade did not amount to much. The distance was too great to ship cattle alive, and the only trade that could be carried on was frozen mutton. The geographical position of Canada, and her nearness to the British market gives her a vast advantage. The manner in which this trade in frozen mutton was conducted by New Zealand, however, showed the way to the Argentine and the United States, when they inaugurated their chilled meat trade. Owing to the distance New Zealand and Australia are from the British market their meat products have to be sent in a frozen state which take from their value about 50 per cent, whereas Canadian meat products are

practically the same value on the British market as fresh slaughtered meat. The embargo placed on cattle by the British government, gave Australia and New Zealand an opportunity to participate in the chilled meat trade, and both these countries have become extensive shippers. New Zealand with her small population now ships about $21,000,000 worth of chilled meat per year; Australia about $10,000,000 worth per year. In 1878, 32 years ago, New Zealand did not ship one dollar's worth.
In these countries, the cattle trade was much in the same position as it is at present in western Canada. The government however, in the face of tremendous depression in trade, and hard times, faced the situation, and these countries, Australia and New Zealand, began establishing cold storage depots throughout the country, where mutton, beef and farm produce could be gathered, chilled and shipped to the British markets. The result has more than justified this paternal action. Business has expended, and to-day we are purchasing New Zealand butter and Australia's chilled and frozen mutton in British Columbia and Alberta.
Now, what lessons are we to learn from the experience of other countries? We know that our trade is adversely affected. We know that that trade is iso affected by the lack of proper transportation facilities. We know now that there is not -sufficient private capital available to take a hold of the business in a proper manner in the west; and we know that, if it should, the farmers and ranchers would soon be in the clutches of trusts, that we would have another Big Six or Big Eight doing the cold meat business for us, and that we would have to take whatever price the dealers chose to pay to us for our live stock.
The conditions which prevail in our western country, with its enormous influx of new settlers, and the great opportunities for speculation, which are open to people with money, are such that it will be impossible to raise money there to establish the necessary facilities for the shipping of meat in proper condition. It is because of the lack of these facilities that the meat industry of that country has sunk to such a deplorable position as it is in to-day, and unless the government sees its way to do something to revive that industry, it i;s going to be in a very bad condition in the near future.
With the examples of these other countries before us, we must come to the conclusion that this government should follow the example of New Zealand or Australia. Cold storage warehouses should be established by the government and the railways should be compelled to supply us with refrigerator cars. This is the only solution of this question. It will take a'
long time for private enterprises to build this trade up as it should be. In the meantime, we may be left hopelessly behind in the markets of the world, as far as chilled meat trade is concerned.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture may say that the number of cattle in the west is not sufficient to justify any expenditure upon cold storage warehouses by the government. If the government showed any disposition to provide these facilities, it would not be very long until there would be plenty of cattle in the west. The growth of the trade of New Zealand and Australia proves this. This is an illustration of the old proverb, where there is a will there is_ a way. If the minister took a proper interest in that country, he would find a way to help the ranchers; and there is no doubt that if he encouraged that business as he might and should, tire supply would, in a short time, be ample to fulfil all the requirements.. There would be no difficulty about the supply if there were only a steady market and a better mode of transportation.
The Prime Minister says that he is opposed to government ownership, but is in favour of government control. I suppose he means by that, that he is not in favour of the government owning utilities, but prefers the trusts to control the government, which is not exactly what he says, but is how it works out.
For my part, I believe in the government establishing these warehouses, and operating them as part of our transportation system. This plan has worked successfully in New Zealand and Australia and there is no reason why it should not work out successfully here. But under present conditions anything is better than nothing.
The western farms, if they are going to be the graneries of the world, must have fertile fields. To accomplish this, we must have cattle raising as well as gra'in growing. In order to succeed in cattle raising we must adopt modern methods, and it is not too much for us to expect or to ask from this government to do what has been done in other colonies successfully, and establish cold storage warehouses in the west, in order to encourage the export of chilled meats to the markets of the world. The farmer then will be pocketing the difference in the freight and the shrinkage which in itself is a very large profit, and Canada will very soon take its former position in the foreign markets as a meat and produce exporting country.

If this government will not do something for the farming interest, that interest is certainly bound to suffer. To a considerable extent, Mr. Speaker, I am in sympathy with the resolution offered by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I am always in sympathy with anything w-hich has a tendency to benefit the farmer. I agree with the hon. gentleman that not enough has been done in the

farming interest, but I am convinced that more has been done than my hon. friend is [DOT]willing to admit. I regret exceedingly the doleful tone in which he introduced his resolution and the despairing view he took with regard to the live-stock of Canada. With his statement of the case I am not at all prepared to agree, and am convinced that the deductions he made from the figures he was able to produce were not warranted. The fact that our export of live-stock has decreased, he considers an indication of the decay and the unprofitableness of the live-stock industry. This is not a correct diagnosis of the case. The fact that less cattle are exported from Canada does not mean at all that our production of cattle has decreased, but what it does mean is that they are being consumed in Canada instead of exported. In proof of this let me point to the facts as I find them in the United States report. The advanced report of their census, taken this year regarding live-stock, would indicate that the number of cattle in the United States has increased by several millions as compared with several years ago ; and yet reading down the Trade -and Commerce report I notice that in 1900 the United States exported to Great Britain and other foreign countries nearly 6,000,000 hundred weight of pork, bacon and other animal products, whereas, in 1909 they exported only some 3,326,000 hundred weight. From Canada I find that in 1900 we exported 748,000 hundred weight and in 1909 only 497,000 hundred weight, which is not nearly the ratio of decrease that occurred in the United States, where notwithstanding the large decrease in exports, the number of cattle had increased as shown by their census so largely in those ten years. It cannot, therefore, be inferred that Canada's production is decreasing in pork, bacon, hams, cattle and sheep and their meat equivalents.
Take the exports of beef from the United States, in 1900 there were 5,693,000 hundred weight exported to Great Britain, and in 1909, 2,404,000 hundred weight, while from the Dominion of Canada the exports were 708,000 hundred weight in 1900 and 715,000 hundred weight in 1909, which would indicate that the increase in cattle and beef and other products had been greater in Canada than in the United States, instead of decreasing as the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has tried to make out, taking our exports as a basis.
Taking the exports to Great Britain of mutton, I find that from the United States, in 1900, 82,000 cwt. were exported, -and in 1909 that had been reduced to 6,000 cwt., whilst in the Dominion of Canada 26,000 cwt. in 1900 had been reduced to 2,000 cwt. in 1909, a decrease quite in correspondence with the decrease in the United States, yet it is claimed that the increase in the United 40
States of live sheep is almost one-eighth in the same period of time, from which I think I can easily conclude that the number of sheep has not decreased in Canada. As a matter of fact, the farmers engaged in livestock and who combine that with other branches of their farming are undoubtedly our most prosperous farmers. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) indicated that in other branches of agriculture there was prosperity among the farmers because of their export of products being larger than that of livestock. That is not the case. Any person conversant with the farming community will know that when he wants to see the most decided indications of prosperity among the farmers he must look almost invariably to those engaged in livestock in some way. Further than that, the financial condition of the livestock men, or those who make livestock a considerable part of their business, is better than that of those engaged in other lines of farming. Notwithstanding the assumption that the livestock industry of our Dominion is going to the dogs, as a matter of fact, there is a decided increase in the interest taken in all branches of livestock, and particularly in the one referred to by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) as being in a very distressed condition-the sheep industry. We find that there is a marked revival in this industry. And there is good reason for it. For a few years past the profits of sheep raising have been much greater than they were before, and this has been an incentive to a large number of farmers to introduce small flocks. Those in the west engaged largely in grain growing are adopting this method. In proof of this I may state that during the present year in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan a number of carloads of sheep have been introduced by the assistance of the livestock associations, which have been assisted in turn by the government. These sheep were sold by auction. Though the promoters of the scheme anticipated that there would be a deficit on the transaction the grain growing farmers were so anxious to secure the foundations of flocks of sheep that there was a profit from the transaction. In every country where grain farming has been carried to -an extreme the impoverishment of the soil has followed. The people, after they have taken the cream from the soil by grain growing, fall back on live stock to revive the soil and bring it into a state of fertility. One of the chief reasons why the livestock interests are prospering is the increase in the price. All kinds of livestock are higher than they were fourteen years ago. Take, for instance, horses. At that time, if we were able to sell them at all, they were bought very largely jor export, and at a very small price. And the number of horses exported and the prices that we obtained at that



time made horses a very considerable item in the exports of farm products. To-day we export scarcely any horses, and yet our production is a great deal larger and the prices we obtain are higher. Now, these horses, instead of being exported, are bought and taken out to western Canada. There they are purchased very largely by the farmers and still more largely, probably, for construction on the great Transcontinental and other railways. The number of cattle exported from the Dominion is undoubtedly considerably less than it was some years ago. There is good reason for this. The price is higher than it was at that time, so that the farmer is actually making more money from the produce of the farm in the shape of cattle than he was at that time. The home consumption is so much greater now than it was then that it absorbs all classes of cattle. The butcher cattle of our Toronto and Montreal markets are selling at almost as high prices as the cattle for export. The reason is that there is not sufficient supply of butcher cattle on the market, and the buyers are obliged to take some of those 'which otherwise would be exported. Then, with regard to the western cattle, as the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) pointed out, so great has been the demand for home consumption that not only have large numbers of cattle been kept here of the class that were formerly exported, but they have taken the feeder class of cattle, which formerly were taken to the country and returned prime export animals and' have used them for consumption in Canada. This has necessitated the importation from the west of a large number of cattle. Hundreds and hundreds of carloads have been brought into Ontario and sold to the Ontario farmers .as feeders. The result has been higher prices for western cattle than have * prevailed in the western provinces for many years.

On this point I think the Minister of Agriculture was quite correct when he said that so far as cold storage transportation is concerned, it is quite equal to the' requirements of the country at the present time. I have no doubt that as the requirements of the country call for greater cold storage facilities, they will be provided by the government. As to the question of abattoirs, or slaughter houses, I think the position of the Minister of Agriculture is quite sound, I do not think the time has yet arrived when the farmers of Canada are able to guarantee a sufficient number of cattle, sheep or swine to warrant the government in expending for abattoirs so large a sum of money as has been mentioned. Some hon. members opposite have spoken of the $8,000,000 proposed to be expended for this purpose as a paltry sum. I consider it as a considerable sum, especially as it would be expended in the way of experiment. As in respect to cold storage facilities, so in respect to abattoirs, I have no_ doubt that just as soon as the necessity arises the government will furnish all the assistance that is required. It is from the province of Alberta that the most urgent requests have come to the government for the establishment of government owned abattoirs. Let me point out that the provincial government of Alberta have been urged very strongly to provide packing houses under government control, or built by the government, for the use of the people. After a considerable amount of discussion the provincial government in 1908 made this proposition, that just so soon as the farmers of Alberta were prepared to guarantee a sufficient number of hogs to warrant the government in providing the packing houses, that would be done, and up to this time no such guarantee has been provided. And yet during these last two years the farmers

of Alberta have been receiving for their hogs a larger price than in any previous year. This I think is an argument in support of the position that the time has not yet arrived when the farmers of the Dominion of Canada are able to guarantee a sufficient number of cattle, sheep or swine to warrant the government in undertaking an enterprise of that kind.
As I said in the beginning of my remarks, I am to a large extent in sympathy with the motion of my hon. friend from East Grey. While I would be willing to support him in any move having for its object the benefit of the farmers, yet, after all that the government of Canada and the Minister of Agriculture have succeeded in doing for the farmers, I would certainly be unwilling to support a motion practically censuring them for not doing anything at all. For this reason I shall be obliged to vote against the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Smith, iunmiie-sex, N.) will forgive me if I do not follow him in his argument, but I shall endeavour to meet some of the points advanced by him as I go along. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) for bringing this matter before the government at this time, because the chilled meat trade in Western Canada is a very important question. The minister said this afternoon that he was pleased and satisfied with the conditions throughout Canada in connection with the dead meat business. If so the hon. gentleman is easily satisfied or else he does not understand the conditions. He practically admitted in his speech this afternoon that as far as his own department is concerned it was a failure, and that he had not been making good as Minister of Agriculture. I would ask him if he has ever had this question of the chilled meat trade investigated in connection with Australia, the Argentine Republic or the United States? This is something that he should do, he should go into it very fully. He said this afternoon that he had always followed out the suggestions made by his employees. I understand that Dr. Rutherford advised the government to establish a cold storage system for chilled meat throughout Canada. I may be wrong in this, but I understand that to be a fact.
The reason for the high price of beef in Canada to-day is that the meat combine of Western Canada and the hog combine of Western Canada have driven the producers out of the business. The minister has been asked time and time again to investigate the meat trade of Canada. Delegation after delegation has come to Ottawa and made this request and in each case the minister has refused to investigate. Then the farmers of Manitoba took the matter up in con-40^
nection with the provincial government ; they asked the Roblin government to investigate it, a provincial commission was appointed, that commission travelled from one end of the province to the other, thoroughly investigating the conditions. Did they find that the farmers were satisfied and making money out of the cattle trade? No, they did not, they found that on every beef that a farmer raised to 3 years old he lost $5.80. They also found that the dealer made $13.60 on each beef, and that the abattoir people or the beef combine of Western Canada made $23.10 on every head of cattle on which the producer was losing $5.80. These are the actual conditions in Western Canada to-day and these are the conditions with which the Minister of Agriculture says he is perfectly satisfied. I am told that in Montreal the public abattoir slaughters the beef and hands it out to the retailer for one dollar a head, but we in Western Canada have to pay $23.10 for the same service. I say it is a shame that such conditions should exist. I represent a rural constituency and I know of lots of farmers throughout my constituency who in the past have kept 50, 75 and 100 head of cattle, but who are now entirely going out of that business because there is absolutely no money in it for them. The scarcity of beef and pork in this country to-day and the high price of these products is due to the driving of these men from the business. The same conditions pertain to Alberta and Saskatchewan as you have been told here to-night. We have to compete not only with the beef combine and the pork combine in Western Canada; even the transportation companies are standing in with these large dealers and opposing everything in connection with a private man shipping cattle in any shape or form. How do they do it? A man will come into a station and ask for cars. The agent will say: Yes, we will have cars here for you on a certain day. The man then drives in his stock, perhaps 300 or 400 head, and he will have to hold these cattle there for days at a time. The transportation companies will not supply the cars as they agreed to do. If any person doubts this statement, let him look at the report of the second general convention of the National Live Stock Association. In it he will find that the conditions are just as I say. They hold the cars back and will not supply them. Then the dealer, the agent of the beef combine, will come along and will offer the man in the first place $27.50 a head for his stock. He refuses to take it and then after a few days the agent returns and offers him $40. There is no car in sight, but the producer refuses this price also. Then they hold him up a day or two longer and the agent offers him $42. He has to take this price because he is feeding this stock with hay at $6, $8

and $10 a ton. This is the way in which we are being held up not only by the beef trust but by the transportation companies as well, and this is the condition with which the minister is satisfied.
The minister has also been asked time and time again to open up new markets. There are resolutions in this report asking him to open new markets, and I would like to know if he has done it, if he has ever made any attempt to open a market for the thoroughbred stock of this country. The Live Stock Association of Canada have again and again asked him to go into the cold storage business and investigate it, and I think it is time the minister was doing something of this kind to assist the cold storage industry-or else he should go to the Senate and allow some other man to do it. The minister's reply is at page 95 of this report. The reason he there gives to the stock men for not going into the cold storage business in this country is not as he has told us here to-day. He says in this report that he will not go into this business because he might have to spend some money in Liverpool. I say it makes no difference where he spends the money of this country if it will relieve the situation and help out the settlers throughout Canada. Seemingly he will not help the producer either at home or abroad.
The Minister of Agriculture has changed a good deal since last year or the year before in stating his reasons why the export of farm products is decreasing year after year. To-day, he says the decrease is because of home consumption, but in 1909 he said it was because the farmers of Canada were slipshod, indifferent, lazy and careless. To-day he has changed his tune. Sir, when the Minister of Agriculture calls the farmers of this country slipshod, lazy and careless he is far beside the mark. I would account for the decrease in our exports because of the fact that the minister and the government have not gone into this question thor-1 oughly and worked ft out to a successful issue as they should have done. Last year or the year before the minister sent a commission to England, Ireland, Scotland, Denmark and Holland to look into the swine business, but he knows as well as I know, and I know as well as he knows, that we can grow as good pork in Canada as can be grown anywhere in the world, and that no pork products bring a higher price on the market than do ours. But, he wanted to give these friends of his a jaunt to the old country and so he sent them off on this commission, which cost' the people of Canada $8,242.11, and I have no hesitation in saying that the report they brought back is absolutely not worth one cent. Again, the minister put the cart before the horse. If he had sent his Mr. SHARPE (Lisgar).
commission to Australia, to the Argentine republic, or to the United States to inquire into how they handle their cold storage and chilled meat business, there might have been some benefit accruing to the country, but as usual, the minister went the wrong way about it. The hon. gentleman from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) said the government should not do this, that, and the other thing, but in my opinion one of the functions of the govern-' ment is to stand between the consumer and the producer to see that there is no undue toll taken by the one from the other, and if they find that one class of our people is being robbed by the other it is their duty to come to the relief of the oppressed. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin) gave us figures some time ago to show the great prosperity of Canada, but he forgot to tell us that the exportation of everything raised and grown on the farms of this country, except wheat,! is decreasing every year. Canada is a farming country, and surely such a condition should not exist. I shall give to the House figures in connection with some of the most important branches of the live stock industry on the farm to show how their exportation is decreasing year by
